werk/depeche-mode-some-great-reward.text:
Some Great Reward is Depeche Mode's fourth studio album, released on 24 September 1984 on Mute Records. Recording began around Christmas 1983, still during the tour for the previous album. They began at Music Works in London, but moved to Hansa Studios in West Berlin, where most of the album took shape. The city had freed the band from its soft image: they now had themselves photographed in black leather. Gareth Jones was now one of the producers.

Here too the group used many samples, in the service of a stronger, more atmospheric sound. People Are People became the band's first number 1 in West Germany, partly thanks to an advertising campaign for the 1984 Olympic Games. Master and Servant and Blasphemous Rumours were also released as singles.
werk/depeche-mode-some-great-reward.listen: Listen to People Are People, the song with which the band first topped the charts in West Germany, and notice the use of samples.

werk/depeche-mode-speak-en-spell.text:
This 1981 debut is the only album with the founder Vince Clarke, who wrote most of the songs, while Martin Gore contributed two. The group consisted of synthesizer players: Clarke, Gore, Andrew Fletcher and the singer Dave Gahan. They signed with Daniel Miller's Mute Records, and Miller co-produced the album with the band. After the singles Dreaming of Me and New Life, the group recorded the rest at Blackwing Studios in London. Because the studio had only eight tracks, it was recorded almost live, with an ARP 2600 and a sequencer. Miller wanted a good electronic pop sound that was not a copy of anything else. Clarke said his lyrics had no message: he thought the sound of the words more important. The title refers to the toy Speak & Spell.

The album reached number ten in England.
werk/depeche-mode-speak-en-spell.listen: Listen to New Life and notice how the synthesizers separately take care of the melody, the bass and the rhythm. Can you hear how simple and yet catchy it sounds together?

werk/depeche-mode-violator.text:
After Music for the Masses, the band set to work in 1989 with the producer Flood, at the suggestion of label boss Daniel Miller. Martin Gore supplied simpler demos, so that the group could do more of the working-out in the studio. They first worked for seven weeks in Milan, then at Puk Studios in Denmark. They were looking for a harder sound, and there is more guitar than on earlier records.

Personal Jesus grew out of a demo with just a beat and a melody on acoustic guitar. For the stomping sound they recorded people jumping on flight cases. According to Flood, the single showed that this was Depeche Mode, but different. The album brought the group international fame, with Personal Jesus, Enjoy the Silence, Policy of Truth and World in My Eyes as singles. It is their best-selling album and appears on lists of the best records of the 1990s.
werk/depeche-mode-violator.listen: Listen to Personal Jesus and notice the stomping rhythm: the sound was made from recordings of people jumping on flight cases.

werk/derek-bailey-guitar-drums-n-bass.text:
Guitar, Drums 'n' Bass was released in 1996 on Avant Records. The guitarist Derek Bailey had spent years improvising over jungle and drum and bass on pirate radio. He suggested to John Zorn that they make an album of it. Zorn found the Birmingham producer D.J. Ninj, who recorded his music in the spring of 1995. A first session with the engineer Mick Harris failed. In October 1995 the guitarist recorded his improvisations over Ninj's music, in Bill Laswell's studio in New York.

The drum and bass sounds booming and minimal, while the guitar is inventive, loud and fast, with broken-off licks, heavy distortion and jangling sounds. The record is regarded as the first combination of free improvisation on guitar and breakbeat music. It received glowing reviews and was the first genre experiment of the late 1990s, when he recorded with unexpected, non-improvising partners.
werk/derek-bailey-guitar-drums-n-bass.listen: Listen to Concrete (Cement-Mix) and notice how the guitar plays short, distorted phrases above the booming rhythm.

werk/derek-bailey-yankees.text:
Yankees is an album of improvised music by the guitarist Derek Bailey, the trombonist George Lewis and the alto saxophonist John Zorn. It was released in 1983 as an LP on Celluloid and later came out on CD, once from vinyl and once on Charly from the original master tape. It was the first time the guitarist and Zorn appeared together on record. In 1993 the two made Harras, together with William Parker. All five pieces are credited to the whole trio.

The record was well received. AllMusic gave it four stars and called its elaborations on the trivia of baseball sounds subtle, dry and hilarious. The Penguin Guide to Jazz counted it among the great improvisation records of the decade, although it increasingly feels like a Zorn project.
werk/derek-bailey-yankees.listen: Listen to Who's on First, the shortest piece, and follow how guitar, trombone and alto saxophone respond to one another in an improvised conversation.

werk/dexter-gordon-a-swingin-affair.text:
A Swingin' Affair is an album by the saxophonist Dexter Gordon, recorded on 29 August 1962 at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey. It was recorded two days after Go, with the same line-up: the pianist Sonny Clark, the bassist Butch Warren and the drummer Billy Higgins. Even so, the album lay on the shelf for two years and was released only in early October 1964 on Blue Note.

Of the six pieces, three are standards. Two were written by the saxophonist himself and one came from Warren. The Penguin Guide to Jazz picked You Stepped Out of a Dream as the highlight, but called the session not entirely gripping.
werk/dexter-gordon-a-swingin-affair.listen: Listen to You Stepped Out of a Dream and notice how the tenor saxophone plays the melody and how the rhythm section swings beneath it.

werk/dexter-gordon-daddy-plays-the-horn.text:
Daddy Plays the Horn is a 1955 jazz album by the tenor saxophonist Dexter Gordon. He plays in a quartet with the pianist Kenny Drew, the bassist Leroy Vinnegar and the drummer Lawrence Marable. The programme consists of six pieces, two of them by Gordon himself: the title song and Number Four. The quartet also plays Confirmation by Charlie Parker, the ballads Darn That Dream and Autumn in New York, and You Can Depend on Me.

Billboard found the album not particularly original, but swinging. The magazine heard in Gordon's playing a firm sound, inspired by Lester Young. The Penguin Guide to Jazz gave it three of four stars and named Confirmation and Autumn in New York as the main reasons to buy the record. The playing of Drew and Vinnegar was also praised.
werk/dexter-gordon-daddy-plays-the-horn.listen: In Autumn in New York, listen to the full sound of the tenor saxophone and notice how piano and bass accompany the playing.

werk/dexter-gordon-doin-allright.text:
Dexter Gordon recorded Doin' Allright for Blue Note in 1961. It was his first record for that label. Gordon plays tenor saxophone in a quintet with the trumpeter Freddie Hubbard, the pianist Horace Parlan, the bassist George Tucker and the drummer Al Harewood. The CD contains two extra tracks: I Want More and an alternate take of For Regulars Only. At just over twelve minutes, Society Red is the longest piece.

In the 1950s Gordon was largely forgotten. The title therefore suits the moment well: here the saxophonist made the first of three successful comebacks. AllMusic gave the album four stars and saw in the Blue Note recordings the occasion for his rediscovery.
werk/dexter-gordon-doin-allright.listen: In Society Red, listen to the interplay of tenor saxophone and trumpet and notice how the rhythm section carries the piece.

werk/dexter-gordon-go.text:
Go was recorded in Chicago in 1959 and released by the label Vee-Jay. The bassist Paul Chambers played with the trumpeter Freddie Hubbard, the alto saxophonist Cannonball Adderley, the pianist Wynton Kelly and the drummer Philly Joe Jones, who on some of the tracks was replaced by Jimmy Cobb. It is hard bop, in which original compositions by Chambers alternate with well-known standards such as Just Friends and I Got Rhythm.

Hubbard was at the start of his career and made one of his first recordings here. A reviewer observed that Hubbard and Adderley may never again have played together in the foreground. Awful Mean was written by Adderley. The record was reissued in 1997 as a double CD with extra recordings and alternate takes.
werk/dexter-gordon-go.listen: Listen to I Got Rhythm and notice how the bass plays a firm line throughout the song, even beneath the horn solos.

werk/diana-ross-everything-is-everything.text:
Everything Is Everything is Diana Ross's second studio album and was released on 3 November 1970 on Motown. After her self-titled debut, containing among others Ain't No Mountain High Enough, the label hurried to make a follow-up. The producers Deke Richards and Hal Davis were instructed to make the album somewhat more pop-oriented than the soulful debut that Ashford & Simpson had produced. The album contains covers of hits by The Beatles and The Carpenters.

The first single, I'm Still Waiting, became a number one hit in England in 1971. Doobedood'ndoobe, Doobedood'ndoobe, Doobedood'ndoo followed and reached number twelve. Her version of I Love You (Call Me), originally by Aretha Franklin, was nominated for a Grammy. The album did not match the successes of the debut, but many fans still saw it as a worthy counterpart. In 2008 an expanded CD appeared with remixes and unreleased recordings.
werk/diana-ross-everything-is-everything.listen: Listen to Come Together, a cover of The Beatles, and notice how the singer makes the song her own. Compare it with the original if you know it.

werk/diana-ross-last-time-i-saw-him.text:
Last Time I Saw Him is Diana Ross's fifth studio album and was released on 6 December 1973 on Motown. Seven arrangers worked on it, among them Gene Page, Michael Omartian, Bob Gaudio and Paul Riser. The album reached number fifty-two in the United States. With it, Ross won the 1974 American Music Award for favourite R&B female artist. It was her last studio record in three years, until Diana Ross in 1976.

The title single was a hit: number one on the Adult Contemporary chart and number fourteen on the Hot 100. The song sounds like a blend of country and Dixieland jazz, a departure from her usual sound. The country singer Dottie West made a version of her own shortly afterwards. The album also contains a cover of Behind Closed Doors, which had earlier been a country hit for Charlie Rich, and of Turn Around from the 1960s.
werk/diana-ross-last-time-i-saw-him.listen: Listen to Last Time I Saw Him and notice the blend of country and Dixieland jazz in the accompaniment.

werk/diana-ross-surrender.text:
Surrender was released in June 1999 and was the third album by the British duo. On this record Tom Rowlands and Ed Simons continued with various electronic styles, including house. The album is more experimental than its predecessors and features guest vocalists such as Noel Gallagher of Oasis, Hope Sandoval of Mazzy Star, Bernard Sumner of New Order and Jonathan Donahue of Mercury Rev.

Let Forever Be is a tribute to The Beatles, Out of Control has a house sound and Hey Boy Hey Girl, the big breakthrough hit, sounds like rave. Of The Sunshine Underground, Rowlands said it should sound like a live band still finding its feet. It is a composite of many recordings, with a crazy passage halfway through that seems to disappear into space. Critics were glowing and the album became the duo's second number one.
werk/diana-ross-surrender.listen: Listen to The Sunshine Underground and notice the moment halfway through when the song suddenly lands in a different, wild atmosphere.

werk/dinah-washington-after-hours-with-m.text:
After Hours with Miss D is a 1954 studio album by the singer Dinah Washington. She sings standards by, among others, Irving Berlin, George and Ira Gershwin, Duke Ellington and Cole Porter, such as Blue Skies, A Foggy Day, Pennies from Heaven and Love for Sale.

She is accompanied by a large group of jazz musicians, among them the trumpeter Clark Terry, the tenor saxophonists Eddie Lockjaw Davis and Paul Quinichette, the pianist Junior Mance, the bassist Keter Betts, the conga player Candido Camero and the drummer Ed Thigpen. Some songs last seven minutes or more, others just over two. The 2004 CD reissue added an extended take of Blue Skies.
werk/dinah-washington-after-hours-with-m.listen: In A Foggy Day, listen to how the singer and the accompanying jazz musicians give each other room in a song of nearly eight minutes.

werk/dinah-washington-dinah-washington-s.text:
Dinah Washington Sings Fats Waller is Dinah Washington's seventh studio album, released in 1957 on the label Emarcy. Verve reissued it in 1990 under the title The Fats Waller Songbook. She sings twelve songs that the jazz pianist, organist and singer Fats Waller wrote or played, such as Ain't Misbehavin', Honeysuckle Rose and Black and Blue.

Bob Shad produced the record and Ernie Wilkins arranged and conducted. The orchestra includes well-known jazz musicians such as the trumpeter Clark Terry, the saxophonist Benny Golson and the trombonist Melba Liston. In Honeysuckle Rose and Everybody Loves My Baby, her then husband, the saxophonist Eddie Chamblee, sings along in playful duets. According to AllMusic, the record combines Waller's lively songs with Washington's expressive singing, which handles the classics with ease and is particularly emotional.
werk/dinah-washington-dinah-washington-s.listen: Listen to Honeysuckle Rose and notice the duet between Dinah Washington and the saxophonist Eddie Chamblee: how do they play with each other?

werk/dinah-washington-for-those-in-love.text:
For Those in Love is a studio album by the American jazz singer Dinah Washington, with arrangements by Quincy Jones. EmArcy Records released it in June 1955 and reissued it in 1991. She sings standards by, among others, Cole Porter, Rodgers and Hart and Dorothy Fields, such as I Get a Kick Out of You, You Don't Know What Love Is and My Old Flame.

The accompaniment comes from a small band including the trumpeter Clark Terry, the saxophonist Paul Quinichette, the pianist Wynton Kelly, the guitarist Barry Galbraith and the drummer Jimmy Cobb. A version of I Could Write a Book was later used in an episode of the television series Ash vs Evil Dead.
werk/dinah-washington-for-those-in-love.listen: In I Get a Kick Out of You, listen to how the vocals relate to the accompaniment in Quincy Jones's arrangements.

werk/dionne-warwick-anyone-who-had-a-hea.text:
Anyone Who Had a Heart is Dionne Warwick's second album. It was released in 1964 on Scepter and produced by Burt Bacharach and Hal David, the writers who had shaped her career since her debut.

The title song became her first top ten hit on the American Billboard Hot 100. Three songs came directly from her first album, Presenting Dionne Warwick from 1963: Don't Make Me Over, This Empty Place and I Cry Alone. They are exactly the same recordings, not new takes or mixes. The album was later reissued on CD in a digitally remastered edition.
werk/dionne-warwick-anyone-who-had-a-hea.listen: In Anyone Who Had a Heart, listen to Warwick's voice and notice how she sings the melody and the words of the title.

werk/dionne-warwick-here-i-am.text:
Here I Am is Dionne Warwick's fifth album and was released on 21 December 1965 on Scepter Records. Burt Bacharach and Hal David produced it, as they mostly did until 1968. Recording took place at Bell Sound Studios in New York.

The title single was heard in the film What's New Pussycat?, but did not reach the top 40 in the United States. The follow-up Looking With My Eyes also missed the chart, despite an appearance on the dance programme Hullabaloo. The third single, Are You There (With Another Girl), did become a hit and reached the top 40. The source also mentions the cheerful Window Wishing and the especially beautiful If I Ever Make You Cry. In This Little Light the singer plays piano herself. On some early copies there were errors on the sleeve, with titles that turned out not to be on the record.
werk/dionne-warwick-here-i-am.listen: Listen to This Little Light and notice the piano: the singer plays it herself, so you hear her here in a role other than just as a voice.

werk/dionne-warwick-make-way-for-dionne-.text:
This is Dionne Warwick's third studio album and was released in August 1964 on Scepter Records. It was her first album on the American album charts, with a top ten place on the R&B chart. The songs mostly come from Burt Bacharach and Hal David, her regular musical partners.

Walk On By was one of the singles and her second top ten hit on the American Billboard Hot 100. You'll Never Get to Heaven If You Break My Heart and A House Is Not a Home are also on it, along with one of the first recordings of They Long to Be Close to You. Get Rid of Him is an old recording by the Shirelles from 1962, on which her voice replaced the vocals of Shirley Alston. A reviewer at AllMusic gave three out of five stars. He wrote that Bacharach and David supplied many songs that later became famous with other singers.
werk/dionne-warwick-make-way-for-dionne-.listen: Listen to Walk On By and notice how the melody builds and how the singer carries the song.

werk/dionne-warwick-presenting-dionne-wa.text:
Presenting Dionne Warwick is the singer's debut album, released by Scepter Records on 10 April 1963. Burt Bacharach and Hal David wrote three quarters of the songs. They had met her in the summer of 1961 at Bell Sound Studios, when she was working as a backing singer on a recording by The Drifters. They would become her regular writers.

The record contains the debut single Don't Make Me Over and Wishin' and Hopin', which became a hit for Dusty Springfield in 1964. Make It Easy on Yourself and the melancholy I Cry Alone also stand out. In Zip-A-Dee-Doo-Dah her sister Dee Dee Warwick and The Shirelles sing along. AllMusic gave four out of five stars and praised her inviting voice and the carefully made material.
werk/dionne-warwick-presenting-dionne-wa.listen: In Don't Make Me Over, listen to Warwick's voice, the heart of the record, and notice how she sings the line of the title.

werk/dire-straits-brothers-in-arms.text:
Recording of Brothers in Arms began on 2 November 1984 at AIR Studios on the island of Montserrat. The singer and guitarist Mark Knopfler had written all the songs and produced the record together with Neil Dorfsman. It was one of the first albums recorded on a digital 24-track machine. The guitarist Hal Lindes left the band early in the sessions, after which Knopfler himself played the majority of the guitar parts.

In Money for Nothing his guitar acquired a striking sound, possibly because of the unusual placement of the microphones. The album was released on 17 May 1985 and was the first album to sell more than a million copies on CD. It stayed at the top of the charts in England, America and Australia for months. The record won a Grammy for best engineering and a Brit Award for best British album.
werk/dire-straits-brothers-in-arms.listen: Listen to Money for Nothing and notice the sound of the guitar at the start of the song. This is the sound Mark Knopfler was looking for in the studio.

werk/dire-straits-communique.text:
Communiqué is Dire Straits' second album and was released on 5 June 1979, eight months after the debut. After the first tour, the band went into the studio in November and December 1978, at Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas. The experienced producers Jerry Wexler and Barry Beckett led the sessions and the mix followed in January 1979 at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Alabama. Beckett also played keyboards on some of the nine songs. It was the last album with David Knopfler and with the original line-up.

Lady Writer was the first single. The album reached number five in the United Kingdom and topped the chart in Germany. Reactions were divided: one reviewer spoke of a competent record, another praised the production on Once Upon a Time in the West, and AllMusic found it a copy of the debut with weaker material.
werk/dire-straits-communique.listen: Listen to Once Upon a Time in the West and notice the vocals and the guitar playing: what atmosphere does the music evoke in you, and does it suit the title?

werk/dire-straits-making-movies.text:
Making Movies is Dire Straits' third album and was released on 17 October 1980. Mark Knopfler wrote the songs in the first half of that year and asked Jimmy Iovine to produce, known for his work with Bruce Springsteen. Iovine also brought in the keyboardist Roy Bittan of the E Street Band. Recording took place at The Power Station in New York. During the sessions David Knopfler left the band; Mark re-recorded his guitar parts. Shortly after the release Alan Clark and Hal Lindes joined, making the group a quintet.

The record contains seven songs. Romeo and Juliet became the biggest single, and Tunnel of Love opens the album with an intro taken from The Carousel Waltz. Rolling Stone wrote that Knopfler stepped out of the shadow of his influences and placed the record at number 52 among the best albums of the 1980s.
werk/dire-straits-making-movies.listen: Listen to Tunnel of Love and notice the beginning: which melody do you hear before the band comes in, and what happens to the atmosphere afterwards?

werk/dirty-three-horse-stories.text:
Horse Stories is the third studio album by the Australian group Dirty Three, released on 10 September 1996 by Touch and Go Records. The record was made at Maison Rouge Studios in London. The guitarist Mick Turner designed the cover. The trio from Melbourne plays instrumental music with violin, drums and guitar.

The album also contains I Remember a Time When Once You Used to Love Me, an adaptation of the Greek song Mia phora thymamai, written by Giannis Spanos and originally sung by Arleta. A reviewer wrote that the group had never been so fierce as here: the music smoulders and sometimes flares up within a single wordless song.
werk/dirty-three-horse-stories.listen: Listen to I Remember a Time When Once You Used to Love Me. Hear how the violin takes the place of the singing voice in this Greek song.

werk/dizzee-rascal-boy-in-da-corner.text:
Boy in da Corner is Dizzee Rascal's debut album and was released on 21 July 2003 on XL Recordings. Around the age of fourteen he became a drum and bass DJ and rapped on pirate radio. At sixteen he made his first single, I Luv U, himself and signed a solo contract with XL. That song is also on the album.

The record combines British garage beats with a distinctly British outlook. Critics heard in his desperate outbursts and focused anger the voice of a younger generation, with lyrics about growing up, about people who do not want to grow up and about dying before you are grown. Fix Up, Look Sharp uses a sample of The Big Beat by Billy Squier. The album won the Mercury Prize in 2003 and brought grime, a movement from British youth circles, to the attention of a worldwide audience. According to Complex, it made him the first international rapper from his country.
werk/dizzee-rascal-boy-in-da-corner.listen: Listen to Fix Up, Look Sharp and notice the sample of The Big Beat by Billy Squier beneath his fast, sharp flow.

werk/dizzee-rascal-maths-english.text:
Maths + English is Dizzee Rascal's third album. It entered at number seven in England, one place higher than Showtime, and went gold. On Wanna Be, Lily Allen sings along, in a nod to the 1976 musical Bugsy Malone: her parts have the same arrangements as So You Wanna Be a Boxer. The American duo UGK take part on Where's da G's, and the rapper himself appeared on their 2007 record. Joss Stone was due to take part on Da Feelin', but the rapper found it too poppy with her chorus.

In 2008 Definitive Jux released the record in America. That version received the new songs G.H.E.T.T.O. and Driving, and a remix of Where's da G's by El-P.
werk/dizzee-rascal-maths-english.listen: In Wanna Be, listen to the parts Lily Allen sings: they follow the same musical line as So You Wanna Be a Boxer from the film Bugsy Malone.

werk/dizzee-rascal-showtime.text:
Showtime is the second album by the grime artist Dizzee Rascal. It was released on 6 September 2004, shortly after his 2003 debut Boy in da Corner. Dream contains a sample of Happy Talk by Captain Sensible from 1982, and Fickle uses Shine by Lamont Dozier from 1974.

The reviews were very good: on Metacritic the record averages 87 out of 100. Rolling Stone called it his most accessible beats so far, and The Guardian heard all kinds of surprising twists behind his restless voice and nervous rhythms. Pitchfork felt it was not a repeat but a strengthening of his qualities, less shocking than the debut but more pleasant to listen to. In England the album went gold.
werk/dizzee-rascal-showtime.listen: In Dream, listen to the sample from Captain Sensible's Happy Talk, a 1982 pop song that ends up here in a very different setting.

werk/dizzee-rascal-the-fifth.text:
Fifth is the fifth studio album by Soft Machine and was released in 1972. It was the first album after the departure of the drummer Robert Wyatt. The band moved further away from the psychedelic and progressive rock of its beginnings, towards jazz fusion.

The record was made in two parts. Side one comes from the 1971 sessions, with Phil Howard on drums. He then left and John Marshall came in, who plays on side two. Roy Babbington, later a permanent member, played double bass as a session musician on all the songs of the second side. Elton Dean played alto saxophone, Mike Ratledge electric piano and organ, Hugh Hopper bass. The title Pigling Bland comes from a children's story by Beatrix Potter.
werk/dizzee-rascal-the-fifth.listen: Listen to Pigling Bland and notice what roles the saxophone and the electric piano play.

werk/dizzee-rascal-tongue-n-cheek.text:
Tongue n' Cheek is the fourth studio album by the British rapper Dizzee Rascal and was released on 20 September 2009. In interviews he let it be known that he was leaving his grime roots behind for more mainstream pop. Calvin Harris produced one track. The album also uses samples: Dirtee Cash takes a piece of Dirty Cash by The Adventures of Stevie V, Can't Tek No More uses Warrior's Charge by Aswad and Chillin' Wiv Da Man Dem takes Oh Honey by Delegation.

Dance Wiv Me, Bonkers, Holiday and Dirtee Disco went to number 1 in the British chart. The reviews were positive. The Guardian still found the distorted synthesizers exciting, and Q called it the first truly big record of British rap. It became the best-selling album of his career.
werk/dizzee-rascal-tongue-n-cheek.listen: Listen to Bonkers and notice the beats and distorted synthesizers, which sound raw and yet bouncy.

werk/dizzy-gillespie-bird-and-diz.text:
Bird and Diz is a studio album by the saxophonist Charlie Parker and the trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie. It was mainly recorded on 6 June 1950 in New York, with Thelonious Monk on piano, Curley Russell on bass and Buddy Rich on drums. It is the last studio record the two made together. In 1952 it was released as a collection of 78 rpm singles on Clef Records, a Verve label.

The producer Norman Granz was known for large line-ups, but here you simply hear the classic bebop format: saxophone, trumpet, piano, bass and drums. Bloomdido opens the record. In 1952 a DownBeat columnist gave the album four stars and wrote that it shows how alive this music still was. The record has been reissued several times, and the CD versions contain extra studio takes.
werk/dizzy-gillespie-bird-and-diz.listen: Listen to Bloomdido and notice how saxophone and trumpet in the bebop format together carry the song.

werk/dj-shadow-endtroducing.text:
Endtroducing..... is DJ Shadow's debut album, released in 1996 by Mo' Wax. He made it over two years, first in his apartment in California and later in Dan the Automator's studio in San Francisco. His equipment was small: an Akai MPC60 MKII, a turntable and an ADAT recorder. He wanted to make a record consisting entirely of samples from vinyl. He sought them mainly in a record shop in Sacramento and preferably chose obscure records, including jazz, funk and psychedelia.

Shadow cut, repeated and stacked the samples into new songs with widely varying moods and tempos. Building Steam With a Grain of Salt revolves around a repeated piano line, to which new sounds are constantly added. Midnight in a Perfect World and Stem became hits in England. Critics praised the album in 1996 and it is now regarded as one of the best records of the 1990s and a milestone of instrumental hip hop.
werk/dj-shadow-endtroducing.listen: In Building Steam With a Grain of Salt, listen to the repeated piano line. Count how many new sounds are gradually added.

werk/doc-watson-home-again.text:
Home Again! is the fourth studio album by the American folk musician Doc Watson and was released in 1966. He plays guitar, twelve-string guitar, banjo and harmonica, and sings. Merle Watson also plays guitar, and Russ Savakus plays bass. The album has fourteen songs, a mixture of traditionals and original work. He wrote two songs together with the fiddler Gaither Carlton, his father-in-law. At just over six minutes, Matty Groves is the longest song.

In Bruce Eder's AllMusic verdict, this is his most moving folk record. Eder praises the surprisingly warm singing voice, which he compares to that of Burl Ives, but rougher. That voice, he says, is often overlooked because the guitar playing attracts so much attention.
werk/doc-watson-home-again.listen: Listen to Matty Groves, the longest song on the album. Notice the voice and how calm the guitar playing stays alongside it.

werk/doc-watson-southbound.text:
Southbound is the second studio album by the American folk musician Doc Watson and was released in 1966. Merle Watson and John Pilla also play guitar on the album, and Russ Savakus plays double bass. After his debut, which consisted mainly of traditional songs, Watson here showed a broader side of himself.

The record mixes traditionals and folk songs with newer material, including a song by Tom Paxton and a song by Mel Tillis and Wayne Walker. There are also original pieces, such as the title song Southbound, written with Merle Watson, and the guitar instrumentals Nothing to It and Nashville Pickin. According to the Allmusic reviewer this was a key album: it showed that Watson could do more than give beautiful interpretations of folk songs. He also wrote strong original work and gave new country songs a compelling twist.
werk/doc-watson-southbound.listen: Listen to Nashville Pickin and follow only the guitar: how fast and clear is the melody Watson plays?

werk/dolly-parton-hello-i-m-dolly.text:
Dolly Parton moved to Nashville in 1964, the day after her high school graduation. At first she wrote songs for others. Fred Foster of Monument Records tried to sell her as a pop singer, but those singles flopped. Only after Bill Phillips had success in 1966 with Put It Off Until Tomorrow was she allowed to record country. In September 1967 her debut appeared, produced by Foster.

She wrote most of the twelve songs herself or together with her uncle Bill Owens. Dumb Blonde came from Curly Putman. Dumb Blonde and Something Fishy became hits, and the album reached number 11 on the Billboard country albums chart. Fuel to the Flame and I'm in No Condition had already been recorded by Skeeter Davis and Hank Williams Jr. AllMusic gave 4.5 out of 5 stars and praised her pronounced personality.
werk/dolly-parton-hello-i-m-dolly.listen: Listen to Dumb Blonde and notice the playful, coquettish tone of the singing.

werk/dolly-parton-in-the-good-old-days-w.text:
In September and October 1968 Dolly Parton recorded this album at RCA Studio B in Nashville, under the producer Bob Ferguson. It was her third solo album for RCA Victor and the first on which she wrote half of the songs herself. That gave her a voice of her own alongside the covers of other people's country hits, such as Harper Valley PTA, D.I.V.O.R.C.E. and The Carroll County Accident.

In the title song she looks back on her poor childhood. She values what that time taught her, but does not want to go back to it. Rolling Stone later called this the first song in which she directly addresses that childhood in the Smoky Mountains. The song was the only single. The album received praise from Billboard, which singled out her empathy in the title song, and reached number 15 on the country chart.
werk/dolly-parton-in-the-good-old-days-w.listen: In In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad), listen to how she sings about the past. Notice whether you can hear in her voice that she values the past and yet does not want to return.

werk/dolly-parton-just-because-i-m-a-wom.text:
In September 1967 Dolly Parton joined Porter Wagoner's show. He also helped her get a contract with RCA Victor. Because her contract with Monument was still running, at first she was only allowed to record duets with Wagoner. Her first solo record for RCA, produced by Bob Ferguson, was recorded in December 1967 at RCA Studio B in Nashville.

She wrote the title song after her husband questioned her about her past. The song was daring for its time: a woman confronts her boyfriend about his judgement, while he had done the same himself. It became the only single and reached number 17 on the Billboard country chart. The Bridge stands out for its subject and for its abrupt ending in the middle of a verse. AllMusic called the record one of her best early albums and praised her as a singer and songwriter.
werk/dolly-parton-just-because-i-m-a-wom.listen: Listen to The Bridge and notice how the story suddenly stops, in the middle of a verse.

werk/dolly-parton-my-blue-ridge-mountain.text:
My Blue Ridge Mountain Boy was Dolly Parton's fourth solo album and the last she recorded in the 1960s. The producer Bob Ferguson recorded it in May and June 1969 at RCA Studio B in Nashville. It became her first solo album in the top ten of the country chart and her first on the Billboard 200.

Many songs tell a story. In the title song a girl from a small town in New Orleans becomes a prostitute and dreams of the boy she left behind. Evening Shade is about an orphanage where the children set fire to the building. In Daddy a daughter begs her father not to leave her mother for a younger woman. There are also covers of In the Ghetto and Games People Play. Billboard called it her best album so far. Rolling Stone later included Evening Shade and the title song in its list of her best songs.
werk/dolly-parton-my-blue-ridge-mountain.listen: In Evening Shade, listen to how the story of the orphanage is told step by step. Notice how the vocals carry the story.

werk/don-cherry-organic-music-society.text:
Organic Music Society was recorded in 1972 for the Swedish label Caprice. The trumpeter Don Cherry works here with a large company: flautists, a sarangi player, percussionists such as Naná Vasconcelos and Okay Temiz, and female singers including his wife Moki Cherry. Besides original pieces, there are compositions by Terry Riley, Pharoah Sanders and Leon Thomas, Dollar Brand and Vasconcelos.

The music mixes avant-garde jazz with influences from the East and from Brazil, in melodic song forms. A reviewer described the Organic Music Society period as the beating heart of Cherry's work, because the music came about collectively. In his view this was the record on which Cherry made himself most fully heard as bandleader and spiritual seeker. Others found the record rather vague and mainly one for fans.
werk/don-cherry-organic-music-society.listen: Listen to Relativity Suite and notice how many different instruments and styles come together in one long piece.

werk/don-cherry-where-is-brooklyn.text:
On 11 November 1966 the cornet player Don Cherry went to Van Gelder Studios in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey. There he recorded this album with Pharoah Sanders on tenor saxophone, Henry Grimes on bass and Ed Blackwell on drums. Blue Note released it.

It is avant-garde jazz in which group interaction matters more than a melody that sticks. The album consists of separate compositions, including The Thing and the almost eighteen-minute Unite. Critics found the music challenging and intense and praised the playing of Sanders and the rhythm section. Some found it less essential than the leader's earlier records, others called it an excellent entry point to the avant-garde. The free jazz trio The Thing named itself after a piece on this album.
werk/don-cherry-where-is-brooklyn.listen: Listen to Unite and notice how the four musicians respond to one another: who leads, who follows and how that keeps changing.

werk/donald-byrd-the-young-bloods.text:
The Young Bloods is an album by the trumpeter Donald Byrd and the alto saxophonist Phil Woods, recorded in 1956 and released on the Prestige label. They are accompanied by the pianist Al Haig, the bassist Teddy Kotick and the drummer Charlie Persip.

The repertoire consists of six pieces. Most come from Woods himself, such as Dupeltook, Once More and House of Chan. There are also two well-known songs: Dewey Square by Charlie Parker and Lover Man, a classic written by Jimmy Davis, Ram Ramirez and James Sherman. Scott Yanow of AllMusic strongly recommended the album to lovers of straight-ahead jazz, even though the record does not last very long.
werk/donald-byrd-the-young-bloods.listen: Listen to Dewey Square and notice how trumpet and alto saxophone relate to each other in this piece by Charlie Parker.

werk/donald-fagen-the-nightfly.text:
The Nightfly was Donald Fagen's first solo album and was released on 1 October 1982. After the break with Walter Becker, his regular partner in Steely Dan, he carried on without him, although he did work with the producer Gary Katz and many well-known session musicians. Recording in New York and Los Angeles took eight months. It was one of the first pop albums to be recorded entirely digitally, which made the work difficult.

Unlike earlier work, the record is strongly autobiographical. The songs are about a childhood in the suburbs of the late 1950s and early 1960s, with late-night jazz programmes on the radio, fallout shelters and the Cuban Revolution. I.G.Y. became a hit and New Frontier was a favourite on MTV. The record was a critical and commercial success and received seven Grammy nominations.
werk/donald-fagen-the-nightfly.listen: Listen to I.G.Y. and notice how polished the sound is: every instrument has its own place and sounds clear.

werk/donna-summer-bad-girls.text:
Bad Girls was released on 25 April 1979 on Casablanca Records, as a double album. Donna Summer, already known as the queen of disco, again worked with Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte, but also with people she had not yet worked with. Because punk and heavy metal were by now also in the charts, the team decided to bring a more rock-oriented sound to some of the songs. Other songs instead got a soul and R&B feel. In this way it became her most varied album so far.

Hot Stuff and Bad Girls open the album, with synthesizers that give the rock sound an electronic, danceable side. Both went to number 1 on the American singles chart, and Hot Stuff earned a Grammy. Dim All the Lights was the third single. The album became one of the most successful of her career, was nominated for Album of the Year and is regarded as one of the best disco albums ever. It was her last studio album for Casablanca.
werk/donna-summer-bad-girls.listen: Listen to Hot Stuff and notice how the guitars and the synthesizers together make a rock-edged and yet danceable sound.

werk/donna-summer-four-seasons-of-love.text:
In October 1976 Donna Summer released Four Seasons of Love, her third concept album. Unlike the previous two, with one long song on side one, this album is more evenly divided. It tells a love story through the four seasons. Side one has Spring Affair and Summer Fever, both disco tracks. Side two has Autumn Changes, somewhat slower, Winter Melody at a slower tempo still, and a reprise of Spring Affair.

Summer was accompanied by the Munich Machine and Giorgio Moroder mixed the album. With the LP came a calendar for 1977 with four photographs, one for each season. The album went gold in the United States and reached number 29 on the Billboard 200. All four songs with a season in the title reached number one on the disco and dance chart.
werk/donna-summer-four-seasons-of-love.listen: Listen to Winter Melody and notice how much slower the tempo is than in the earlier disco tracks.

werk/donna-summer-lady-of-the-night.text:
Lady of the Night is the debut album of the singer Donna Summer and was released on 26 February 1974 in the Netherlands, on Groovy Records. In 1973 she sang backing vocals on an album by Three Dog Night. In the studio she met the songwriters and producers Pete Bellotte and Giorgio Moroder, who saw her talent and offered her a record of her own. Bellotte produced, and together with Moroder he wrote almost the whole repertoire.

Most of the songs are pop and folk pop. The singles The Hostage and Lady of the Night became minor hits in the Netherlands. The Hostage reached the top three in Belgium and Spain, Lady of the Night the top ten in Austria. The album itself did not make any chart.
werk/donna-summer-lady-of-the-night.listen: In The Hostage, listen to the voice of the then unknown singer and to how she carries this pop song.

werk/donna-summer-love-to-love-you-baby.text:
Love to Love You Baby is Donna Summer's second album and the first to be released internationally, on 27 August 1975. In the summer of 1974 she came to Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte with an idea for a song. Moroder wanted to develop a new disco sound and turned it into a distinctly sensual disco track. The label Casablanca asked for a version of almost twenty minutes, and it came to seventeen. That filled the whole of the first side of the record. With the stomping bass drum, Moroder and Bellotte laid the foundation for Eurodisco.

The title song reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 in early 1976, although some radio stations did not play it because of its explicit content. The second side had more soul and R&B, with the ballads Full of Emptiness and Whispering Waves.
werk/donna-summer-love-to-love-you-baby.listen: In Love To Love You Baby, listen to the stomping bass drum that runs beneath the whole song.

werk/donovan-fairytale.text:
Fairytale is the second album by the Scottish singer-songwriter Donovan. Pye released it on 22 October 1965 in the United Kingdom; in the United States a slightly different version appeared in November on Hickory, with Universal Soldier added and Oh Deed I Do removed. Peter Eden, Geoff Stephens and Terry Kennedy produced. As on his debut, Donovan plays harmonica and acoustic guitar; Shawn Phillips plays extra twelve-string guitar.

The music moves further towards British folk, especially in Summer Day Reflection Song and Jersey Thursday. Sunny Goodge Street points ahead to the jazzy atmosphere and the descriptions of London city life that Donovan would continue to explore over the next two years. Record World called that song one of rare beauty.
werk/donovan-fairytale.listen: In Sunny Goodge Street, listen to the jazzy atmosphere and notice the images of London city life in the lyrics.

werk/donovan-sunshine-superman.text:
In 1965 Donovan wanted to shed his folk image, after being accused of copying Bob Dylan. After the end of his relationship with Linda Lawrence he wrote songs in which he wanted to win her back. With the producer Mickie Most and the arranger John Cameron he began work on Sunshine Superman at Abbey Road on 19 December 1965. The word sunshine in the title was slang for LSD. The arrangement with bass, harpsichord, drums and electric guitars, including by Jimmy Page, is regarded as one of the first psychedelic recordings.

The record was released on 26 August 1966 in the United States, but not in Britain because of a contract dispute. Chamber orchestra arrangements of strings and woodwinds colour Bert's Blues and Legend of a Girl Child Linda, which lasts almost seven minutes. The second phase of recording took place in Los Angeles. The record reached number 11 on the American chart and was his biggest success there.
werk/donovan-sunshine-superman.listen: Listen to Sunshine Superman and notice the bass and the harpsichord, which make this song sound different from ordinary folk.

werk/donovan-the-hurdy-gurdy-man.text:
The sixth studio album by the Scottish singer and writer Donovan was released in October 1968 on Epic in North America. In the United Kingdom it did not come out because of a contract dispute. Recording began in January 1968. In February Donovan travelled to Rishikesh in India to learn Transcendental Meditation with the Beatles. There he wrote many new songs. He also taught John Lennon a way of picking the guitar that returns on the Beatles' White Album.

The record is more eclectic than any of his other albums. Jennifer Juniper has strings and flute, A Sunny Day and The River Song sound pastoral, Peregrine and Tangier revolve around drones, and Get Thy Bearings has jazz influences. The title song combines Celtic folk with hard rock and reached the top five in both England and America. John Paul Jones made the arrangement.
werk/donovan-the-hurdy-gurdy-man.listen: Listen to Hurdy Gurdy Man and notice how the acoustic guitar and the heavy, rocking accompaniment together make one sound.

werk/donovan-what-s-bin-did-and-what-s-b.text:
This is the debut album of the Scottish singer-songwriter Donovan, released on 14 May 1965 on Pye. At the end of 1964 Peter Eden and Geoff Stephens had offered him a contract. He was already known in British folk circles. His 1964 demos resembled Woody Guthrie and Bob Dylan strongly, which earned him the nickname Britain's answer to Dylan. On the album his style is already beginning to diverge. He re-recorded Catch the Wind for the record.

He sings and plays harmonica and acoustic guitar, as in his live performances. Car Car is a song by Guthrie, Tangerine Puppet is British folk and Cuttin' Out contains jazz elements. The album reached number 3 in the United Kingdom. In the United States it was released under the title Catch the Wind.
werk/donovan-what-s-bin-did-and-what-s-b.listen: In Catch the Wind, listen to the combination of voice, acoustic guitar and harmonica.

werk/dr-dre-2001.text:
With 2001, Dr. Dre returned in November 1999 with his second solo album, after The Chronic from 1992. He had something to prove: the media doubted whether he could still produce. The title changed several times because of a dispute over the name Chronic with Death Row Records. He and Mel-Man produced most of it. The album was conceived like a film, with build-up, moving and aggressive moments. The collaboration with the keyboardist Scott Storch began here. With piano and strings he brought a new colour.

The sound builds on the G-funk of his debut, with sparse beats, ominous strings, soulful vocals and even reggae. Still D.R.E., Forgot About Dre and The Next Episode became singles. Critics praised the production and the tight beats, but often found the lyrics about violence, drugs and sex too crude. Many critics called The Message, a song for his late brother, the best thing the album could have been.
werk/dr-dre-2001.listen: Listen to Still D.R.E. and notice the piano motif and the sparse beat: how much space does the production leave open?

werk/dr-dre-compton.text:
Compton is Dr. Dre's third album and the follow-up to 2001 from 1999. It came out after he announced in his radio show on 1 August 2015 that he was scrapping the album Detox, which had been delayed for years. During the making of the film Straight Outta Compton, about N.W.A, he became so inspired that he went back into the studio. The work was recorded from 2013 to 2015 with many producers and a long list of guests, among them Kendrick Lamar, Ice Cube, Eminem, Snoop Dogg and Anderson .Paak.

The record was released on 7 August 2015 on Apple Music and iTunes, two weeks before the physical release. Critics were enthusiastic. Rolling Stone called the album at once confusing and compelling, with Dre's ambitious production as a strong point. Robert Christgau named Genocide and Animals as highlights. Pitchfork placed it at number 32 among the best albums of 2015.
werk/dr-dre-compton.listen: Listen to Genocide and notice the guests: which voices do you hear, and how do they relate to the beat beneath?

werk/dr-dre-the-chronic.text:
The Chronic was Dr. Dre's first solo album, after he had left N.W.A and Ruthless Records following a dispute over money. It was released in December 1992 on Death Row Records and was recorded in Los Angeles. On twelve of the sixteen songs Snoop Dogg raps, heard widely here for the first time. Daz Dillinger, RBX and Kurupt were also introduced to the public. The lyrics contain jibes at Eazy-E and Ice Cube.

The production samples little, usually one or a few fragments per song. It makes room for heavy synthesizer basses imitating Parliament-Funkadelic, a lone keyboard line and live instruments. The slow, smooth beats are known as G-funk. Nuthin' But A "G" Thang reached number two on the American singles chart. The lyrics caused uproar over sexism and violence. The record is regarded as highly influential and has been added to the National Recording Registry.
werk/dr-dre-the-chronic.listen: Listen to Nuthin' But A "G" Thang and notice the low synthesizer bass and the relaxed tempo at which the two rappers rhyme in turn.

werk/dr-feelgood-be-seeing-you.text:
Be Seeing You is Dr. Feelgood's fifth album and was released in October 1977. It was the first album after the departure of Wilko Johnson, with the guitarist Gypie Mayo in his place. Nick Lowe produced. The title is a catchphrase from the cult series The Prisoner, which was enjoying a new popularity at the time. The cover plays on this: it bears the text produced by Number 2 for Number 6, the band wear blazers with piping and scarves, and badges came with it. The photograph for the front was taken in the band's own pub, the Admiral Jellicoe.

The songs are short, often around two to three minutes, and consist of original work and covers, including by Nick Lowe, Johnny Guitar Watson and Isaac Hayes. She's a Wind Up became the group's second song on the British singles chart. In October 1977 the album reached number 55 on the British albums chart and stayed there for three weeks.
werk/dr-feelgood-be-seeing-you.listen: Listen to She's a Wind Up and notice how short and direct the song is: it lasts only just over two minutes.

werk/dr-feelgood-down-by-the-jetty.text:
Down by the Jetty is the debut album of the English band Dr. Feelgood and was released in January 1975. Vic Maile produced the record. The group, built around the singer Lee Brilleaux and the guitarist Wilko Johnson, plays original songs influenced by Johnny Kidd & the Pirates, such as Keep It Out of Sight, and also covers such as Boom Boom by John Lee Hooker. Johnson himself wrote almost all the other songs. In 2006 an expanded reissue appeared.

The record had a long afterlife. Paul Weller and Bob Geldof cite it as an influence, and Blondie, the Ramones and Richard Hell also knew it. Weller's band The Jam recorded a demo of Cheque Book in 1976, before it had a contract. In 2006 the magazine Uncut placed the album at number 87 among the best debut albums.
werk/dr-feelgood-down-by-the-jetty.listen: Listen to Boom Boom and notice the guitar of Wilko Johnson, who also does the vocals here himself.

werk/dr-feelgood-malpractice.text:
Malpractice is the second album by the English band Dr. Feelgood and was released in October 1975. In November it reached number 17 on the British albums chart and stayed in that chart for six weeks. It was their first record to make the chart, almost two years before their first single, Sneakin' Suspicion in June 1977. With their narrow suits, short hair and surly attitude, they were among the groups who paved the way for punk.

The record contains songs by the guitarist Wilko Johnson, such as Back In the Night and Another Man, alongside covers such as I Can Tell and Riot In Cell Block Number Nine. The singer Lee Brilleaux sings and plays harmonica, and Bob Andrews plays piano and keyboards as a guest. In 1990 the record was reissued by Grand Records.
werk/dr-feelgood-malpractice.listen: Listen to Back In the Night, a song by Wilko Johnson, and notice how the guitar drives the tempo.

werk/dr-feelgood-sneakin-suspicion.text:
Sneakin' Suspicion is the fourth album by the English band Dr. Feelgood, from 1977. During the recording the group was on the point of falling apart, because the guitarist, songwriter and focal point Wilko Johnson was leaving. Bert de Coteaux produced. Even so it became a British hit: in June 1977 the album reached number 10 on the albums chart and stayed there for six weeks. The title song was the band's first single on the British chart.

Johnson wrote most of the songs. There are also covers, such as Nothin' Shakin' (But the Leaves on the Trees), Lights Out, You'll Be Mine by Willie Dixon and Hey Mama, Keep Your Big Mouth Shut. In the United States the band found no audience. After this album it did not release a record there until 1980.
werk/dr-feelgood-sneakin-suspicion.listen: Listen to Lights Out, at under two minutes one of the shortest songs, and notice how quickly the band gets to the point.

werk/drake-nothing-was-the-same.text:
Drake began work on his third album in 2012, shortly after Take Care. He moved to Los Angeles and said that he now felt content and proud. Marvin Gaye was a major inspiration, especially the album Here, My Dear. Drake did not want to make a pure rap record, but songs with more ballads. The work was mainly made by 40 and other OVO Sound producers, such as Boi-1da, Nineteen85 and Detail. Guests included Jay-Z, Jhené Aiko and Majid Jordan. Seven songs were released as singles, among them Started from the Bottom and Hold On, We're Going Home.

The album received mostly positive reviews and on release went to number one on the American chart. Many magazines counted it among the best records of 2013. It received a Grammy nomination for best rap album.
werk/drake-nothing-was-the-same.listen: Listen to Hold On, We're Going Home and notice how soft and melodic this song sounds, unlike an ordinary rap song.

werk/drake-scorpion.text:
Scorpion is Drake's fifth studio album and his first double album, released on 29 June 2018. The first disc is mainly hip hop, the second R&B and pop. He made it with 40 and his manager Oliver El-Khatib. Just before, he had been in conflict with Pusha T, whose diss track claimed he had a secret child. This is addressed on Scorpion, and later he acknowledged having a son. According to critics, the title was an answer to his opponents.

The lyrics deal with fear, relationships and his path from underdog to top artist. The production draws on soul, ambient, quiet storm, R&B, pop, electronica and trap. Seven singles were released, of which God's Plan, Nice for What and In My Feelings reached number 1. Critics appreciated the songs, but found the whole too long.
werk/drake-scorpion.listen: Listen to God's Plan and notice how sparse the accompaniment is and how the singing and rapping alternate.

werk/drake-take-care.text:
After Thank Me Later in 2010, Drake felt dissatisfied with the coherence of his debut album. He considered it rushed and called his second album Take Care because he could now take his time. He worked intensively with his regular producer Noah 40 Shebib, who did most of the production, with contributions from, among others, T-Minus, Boi-1da and Jamie xx of The xx. The album was mainly recorded in Toronto and came out on 15 November 2011.

It sounds slow, sensual and dark, with minimalist R&B, and Drake alternates between singing and rapping. The lyrics deal with fame, love, money and friendship, full of bravado and vulnerability. Guests include The Weeknd, Rihanna and Kendrick Lamar. Despite a leak nine days before release, the album topped the Billboard 200. Critics praised the spacious production and the emotional themes. It won the Grammy for Best Rap Album.
werk/drake-take-care.listen: Listen to Marvins Room and notice the atmosphere of the song and how Drake switches between singing and talking.

werk/drake-thank-me-later.text:
After the success of the mixtape So Far Gone and the song Best I Ever Had, Drake signed with Universal Motown. From 2009 to 2010 he worked on his debut album, at dozens of places from Toronto to Honolulu, and sometimes even on a tour bus. His regular producers 40 and Boi-1da made most of the music. The sound is slow and atmospheric, with sombre synthesizers, sparse beats and soft arrangements. Drake raps and sings quietly about doubt, insecurity, love and his first experiences of fame. In Fireworks he mentions his parents' divorce, and in Karaoke keyboards from the 1980s are heard.

The album was long awaited and went to number one on the American chart. Critics appreciated the personal themes and compared the record with 808s & Heartbreak by Kanye West. The album received a Grammy nomination.
werk/drake-thank-me-later.listen: Listen to Karaoke and notice the keyboards, which sound like 1980s pop, while Drake sings about the effort love takes.

werk/drake-views.text:
Views is Drake's fourth studio album, released on 29 April 2016. He and his regular producer 40 were executive producers, and 40 also did most of the production, together with, among others, Nineteen85 and Kanye West. The title was at first Views from the 6, a reference to Toronto. On the cover he sits on top of the CN Tower. Recording ran from 2015 to 2016.

The sound leans on Caribbean and African music. It is his first real foray into dancehall, alongside R&B, trap, Afrobeats, UK funky and pop. The lyrics deal with love, betrayal and loyalty. Five singles were released, including One Dance, which topped the American Hot 100. Critics were lukewarm and found the album too long. Even so it became one of his biggest commercial successes.
werk/drake-views.listen: Listen to One Dance and notice how a dancehall-like rhythm with a soft melody makes a calm, smooth song.
